source_testimonies.care:
Care-Ethics Reading of the Scenario  

1. What relationships are actually in play?  
• The five people: They are already in harm’s path and, whether they know it or not, are in a position of urgent dependency on anyone nearby who can help.  
• The one person on the side track: At the moment you consider pulling the lever, that individual is not yet endangered; pulling the lever would place them in a danger that you yourself create.  
• You (the bystander): You have not promised, contracted with, or been formally entrusted by any of the six. Still, once you notice the crisis you are morally “addressed” by all of them through their shared human vulnerability.  

2. Comparing the two possible actions through care-ethical dimensions  

           ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
           │          Not Pull (five die)           Pull (one dies)          │
┌──────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Attentive│ Failure to respond to the most urgent│ Active attention to all six;  │
│ ness     │ need of five; risk of moral inattent-│ but new danger introduced for │
│          │ iveness (E1).                        │ one.                         │
├──────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Direct   │ No new vulnerability created, but   │ You create direct, lethal     │
│ Entrust- │ you leave existing dependency unmet.│ vulnerability for the one.    │
│ ment     │                                      │                               │
├──────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Depend-  │ Five remain dependent and abandoned.│ You honor dependency of five, │
│ ency     │                                      │ override safety of one.       │
├──────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Trust &  │ Little interpersonal trust invoked  │ By acting, you implicitly ask │
│ Agency   │ or broken—you remain passive.       │ the one to “trust” a decision │
│-created  │                                      │ you made without their consent│
│ Vulnera- │                                      │ (agent-created vulnerability).│
│ bility   │                                      │                               │
├──────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Respons- │ Responsiveness deficit toward five. │ Responsiveness surplus toward │
│ iveness  │                                      │ five, deficit toward one.     │
└──────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  

3. Role of numbers  
Numerical magnitude (five vs. one) = SECONDARY.  
Reason: The six people stand in roughly symmetrical, impersonal relations to you. Because no deeper tie tips the scale, the greater number intensifies the urgency of their common dependency but does not itself settle the caregiving duty (per instruction: “counts may inform competent and responsive care, but they are decisive only when the competing relational claims are otherwise comparable”). Here the claims are, in fact, comparable, so numbers legitimately matter, but only after all relational considerations have been weighed.

4. Care-ethical tension  
• Not pulling neglects an urgent, preventable harm to five people who are already exposed.  
• Pulling lever actively manufactures a lethal harm for a new person who had no prior dependency on you. This is an instance of agent-created vulnerability—a particularly weighty care concern because care calls us to avoid harming those who have not already been placed in our charge (E2).

5. Is one duty clearly stronger?  
These two care duties (responding to five existing dependencies vs. not creating a new lethal dependency for one) point in opposite directions. Classical care theory gives no clean hierarchy here; both sets of people make morally significant claims on you. Thus:

Care-Ethics Status: NORMATIVELY_CONTESTED.  

Provisional Judgment  
If you give slightly greater moral weight to not being the author of a new fatal vulnerability, you would refrain from pulling the lever.  
If, however, you reason that responsiveness to already imminent large-scale harm is the primary expression of competent care, you would pull the lever.  

Given the symmetry of prior relations and the absence of any special entrustment, many care theorists lean toward acting—precisely because failing to respond looks like a collapse of attentiveness and competence (E1) toward five vulnerable persons. Yet this remains a contested conclusion within care ethics.

Concise Recommendation  
Because the relational claims are roughly equal and care ethics does not rank them definitively, choose either action only after consciously acknowledging the life you would be forsaking or endangering. Whichever course you take, remain ethically answerable: mourn, seek repair where possible, and stay vigilant to future crises so that care may be exercised without having to create new harms.
[/INST]

source_testimonies.deontological:
Action label: PULL_LEVER  
1. Maxim: “When I can avert five certain deaths by diverting an identical threat, I will redirect it even though one innocent will be struck instead.”  Universal-law test: rational agents could will the rescue aspect, yet many could not will being deliberately placed in lethal harm whenever they happen to be the one—indicating a contradiction in the will.  
2. Satisfies: rescue, impartiality.  Violates: non-instrumentalization (one is made the controllable point of impact), autonomy, justice (unequal distribution of protection).  
3. PROHIBITED by the stringent duty not to kill the innocent.  
4. Duty conflict: perfect duty not to kill vs. imperfect duty to aid.  Priority rule: perfect duties override imperfect ones.  
5. Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY—shows the breadth of the rescue duty but cannot override a perfect duty.  

Action label: REFRAIN_FROM_PULLING  
1. Maxim: “When deadly harm is already moving toward five and any redirection would kill an uninvolved person, I will refrain from intervention.”  Universal-law test: all can rationally will not being forced into lethal sacrifice; no contradiction arises.  
2. Satisfies: non-instrumentalization, autonomy, justice.  Violates: rescue, impartiality (fails to aid the five).  
3. REQUIRED, because it honors the superior perfect duty not to kill.  
4. Same conflict; resolved identically—perfect over imperfect.  
5. Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY.  

Deontological Status: Although some Kantians argue the one is not used as a mere means, the prevailing priority of perfect over imperfect duty makes refraining obligatory; pulling is prohibited.
source_testimonies.rawlsian:
Action labels compared: 1) PULL_LEVER, 2) DO_NOT_PULL.

Basic liberty at stake: equal right to life.

Least-advantaged group under each action
• PULL_LEVER: the single redirected victim (faces certain death).  
• DO_NOT_PULL: the five people on the main track (face certain death).

Relative position
Both least-advantaged groups lose the same basic liberty (life). Their position is identical in kind, not magnitude.

Numerical magnitude: IRRELEVANT. Because the loss concerns an equal basic liberty, E2 bars us from trading one person’s inviolable right to life for a greater aggregate benefit to others. Headcount does not license sacrificing a liberty equally owed to each.

Rawlsian comparison
• PULL_LEVER actively violates one person’s inviolable basic liberty in order to spare others.  
• DO_NOT_PULL refrains from directly infringing anyone’s liberty, though five will still die from an external cause.

Since no action can save every life, the primary test is whether an agent may override one individual’s basic liberty to secure the same liberty for others. E2 decisively forbids such deliberate infringement.

Rawlsian Status: FAVOR_ACTION_DO_NOT_PULL. The inviolability of each person’s basic liberty takes priority over numerical gain; therefore justice as fairness rules out PULL_LEVER.
[/INST]

source_testimonies.utilitarian:
Action–Consequence Table (all probabilities ≈1 unless noted)

1. Pull the lever  
a. Five people on main track: survival → +5 lives, high benefit, lifelong, irreversible, STATED  
b. One person on side track: death → –1 life, great harm, irreversible, STATED  
c. Families/friends of saved five: grief avoided → benefit, magnitude large, INFERRED  
d. Family/friends of one killed: new grief → harm, magnitude large, INFERRED  
e. You: possible guilt/gratitude mix, moderate, reversible, UNKNOWN  

2. Do not pull  
a. Five people: death → –5 lives, harm, irreversible, STATED  
b. One person: survival → +1 life, benefit, irreversible, STATED  
c. Families/friends pattern mirrors above (signs reversed), INFERRED  
d. You: possible guilt for inaction, UNKNOWN  

Ranking by expected impact  
Death or survival of each person dominates all secondary effects (death = magnitude –1 life unit).  
Pull lever: net change = +4 life-units (–1 +5).  
Do not pull: net change = –4 life-units.  

Edgeworth’s dictum (E1) directs us to maximize the sum of pleasures; saving four extra lives clearly increases that sum. Mill (E2) allows overriding the right not to be killed when greater utility is at stake. Bentham (E3) grounds the judgment solely in outcomes.

Missing information that could reverse the ranking: if the single person’s continued life would generate ≥4 times the well-being of each of the others combined, or if the five were certain to die imminently anyway. Scenario provides no such data, so these remain speculative.

Utilitarian Status: PULL THE LEVER, conditional on no contrary information about disproportionate future utility of the individuals.
source_testimonies.virtue:
Action A: “Pull the lever”  
Role: a by-standing rail-switch operator de facto.  
Virtues expressed: compassion (protecting five), civic responsibility, decisive courage.  
Vices risked: hubris (playing fate-dealer), callousness toward the one.  
Practical-wisdom notice: absence of consent, instant timing, foreseeable lethal redirection, your unique capacity to act.  
Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY—saving more lives strengthens the compassion case but does not itself ground virtue.

Action B: “Do not pull the lever”  
Role: witness who refrains from lethal redirection.  
Virtues expressed: respect for non-maleficence, humility before tragic limits.  
Vices risked: cowardice (inaction), indifference to preventable deaths.  
Practical-wisdom notice: omission still allows foreseeable harm, but you avoid direct killing.

Central virtue conflict: active compassion & civic courage (A) versus non-maleficence & humility (B).  

Practical-wisdom comparison rule: prefer the act that integrates most virtues while minimizing grave vice, given the agent’s unique situational authority.

Deliberation: Courageous, compassionate intervention (A) better secures communal flourishing and models responsible agency; attendant hubris is containable by humble sorrow and later accountability.

Virtue-Ethics Status: PROVISIONALLY_FAVORS “Pull the lever.”
